title: Speculative Speculative Decoding
one_liner: Instead of waiting for each prediction step before guessing the next, guess many possible paths ahead of time and pick one when verification arrives.
lead: Generating text in a large language model is bottlenecked because each token (a word or fragment) must be produced one at a time. Speculative decoding speed this up by using a fast draft model to guess the next few tokens, then checking them all at once in the big slow target model. Saguaro takes this further: while the target model is checking one set of guesses, the draft model guesses many possible futures at the same time, caches them, and picks one instantly if the check confirms a path it already guessed.

problem.h2: Why generating text one token at a time is painfully slow
paras: When a language model generates text, it works step by step: guess the first word, then based on that word guess the second, then the third, and so on. Each guess requires a forward pass (running the entire neural network). This is purely sequential — you cannot guess word three until word two is decided, even though the model would theoretically do almost the same computation for all three at once.

A naive approach: just run the big model K times to get K tokens at once. This works but wastes time on a slow model that does not need to run this many times; we only need its opinion on a few high-uncertainty spots.

Speculative decoding fixed this by using two models: a fast draft model guesses several tokens ahead, then the target model checks them all in one parallel forward pass. This buys latency (time to produce one token). But there is a remaining sequential dependence: the draft cannot prepare its next guess until it sees which tokens the target accepted or rejected.

callout.html: Speculative decoding still waits for the target to verify before the draft can plan the next batch of guesses.

panels.title: 1. Autoregressive baseline
panels.caption: Model guesses one token, waits, guesses next. Each step is sequential.

panels.title: 2. Speculative decoding
panels.caption: Draft guesses tokens fast. Target checks them in parallel. Still must wait before next draft.

panels.title: 3. Draft pre-computes futures
panels.caption: While verifying, draft pre-guesses many outcomes: accepted counts and bonus tokens.

panels.title: 4. Verification arrives
panels.caption: Target checks result. Draft looks it up in cache. Already have the answer.

panels.title: 5. Zero speculation overhead
panels.caption: Speculations returned instantly if cached. Draft and target run truly in parallel.

steps.text: Before verification starts, the draft model computes speculations for many possible verification outcomes.
While the target model checks the current guess, the draft model is not blocked; it has already prepared.
Target model returns how many tokens were accepted and which bonus token was sampled.
If this outcome is in the cache, return the pre-computed speculation immediately.
If outcome is not cached, run a backup draft to generate it, then proceed to next round.

paras: Speculative decoding has a secret wait: after verification finishes, the draft model must speculatively generate the next batch from scratch, which is sequential. Saguaro eliminates this wait by pre-computing thousands of possible next batches during verification and storing them in a cache.
object.object: Speculation timing: from after verification to during verification

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: Cache hit rate
hidden.name: Fraction of verifications that land in the cache
paras: A cache hit is when the verification outcome (how many tokens were accepted, which bonus token was sampled) matches something the draft model already predicted and cached. A hit means zero overhead — the speculation is returned immediately. A miss means the draft must fallback and re-generate, which costs latency.

The paper estimates this by analyzing which verification outcomes are most likely given the draft model's logits (its confidence scores for each token). It pre-computes speculations for the top outcomes: the ones that verification is most likely to produce. This is done using constrained optimization: given a budget of cache entries, allocate them to the verification outcomes that the draft is most confident will occur.

heat.caption: Darker outcomes are more likely to occur and get cached. Light outcomes are rare, skipped to save space.

reads.html: The cache holds pre-computed guesses for the most likely verification outcomes. If reality matches a guess, instant return.
The cache hit rate is bounded by how well the draft model's logits predict verification outcomes; Theorem 15 shows it increases as the sampling scheme C decreases (favoring more likely outcomes).

mechanism.h2: Why pre-caching speculations eliminates the bottleneck
paras: Standard speculative decoding works like this: draft model runs on a fast device, target runs on a slow device. They are sequential: draft predicts, then target verifies. The target takes 100 milliseconds. During those 100ms, the draft is idle waiting. Then draft generates again (takes 10ms), then target verifies again. The total is 110ms per round.

Saguaro runs them in parallel. During the target's 100ms verification, the draft model is not idle — it is computing many possible futures at once and caching them. By the time verification finishes and returns its outcome, the draft has already computed the answer for that outcome. The outcome lookup takes microseconds. Now both models run together: total time is still 100ms but you generate more tokens, so per-token latency is lower.

The draft model can afford to do many speculations at once because they are independent forward passes. It costs compute but not latency, since they run in parallel with verification. If the draft pre-computes the 10 most likely outcomes out of 1000 possible, and verification actually produces one of those 10 outcomes 90 percent of the time, then 90 percent of the time there is zero overhead.

stages.s: Current state: tokens accepted so far, draft model ready on GPU, target model ready on GPU
Draft generates K candidate tokens and sends to target
While target verifies (100ms), draft pre-generates speculations for top-M verification outcomes
Target returns outcome: how many accepted, which bonus token
Cache lookup (microseconds): return pre-computed speculation or fallback
Next batch of speculations ready, ready for next verification round

math.words: Speedup from Saguaro is approximately: (latency of target model forward pass) divided by (latency of target pass plus expected cost of draft fallback, weighted by cache miss rate)
symbols: time for target model to verify one batch (milliseconds, fixed)
time for draft to generate when cache misses (milliseconds, amortized)
fraction of verifications that hit the cache (a number between 0 and 1)
miss rate: how often fallback is needed

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose T_target = 100 ms (target is slow), T_fallback = 5 ms (draft fallback is fast), and p_hit = 0.9 (cache hits 90% of the time).
That is almost no speedup; the fallback overhead kills it. But if p_hit = 0.99, speedup = 100 / 100.05 = 0.9995x ≈ 1x, meaning you get the parallelism benefit.
If p_hit = 1.0 (perfect cache), speedup = 100 / 100 = 1.0x; draft is free, target is the only cost, and you scale token generation 2-5x (the paper's claimed improvement).

math.note: When cache hit rate is high, fallback cost is negligible, and the draft model becomes free. The paper's key challenge is raising hit rate to this threshold via smart pre-caching.

charts.title: Autoregressive baseline
charts.note: Each token is sequential. Total time grows linearly with token count.

charts.title: Speculative decoding (standard)
charts.note: Draft and target overlap, but fallback re-generation after verification is sequential.

charts.title: Saguaro (Speculative Speculative Decoding)
charts.note: Cache hits eliminate re-generation overhead. Both models run in parallel almost all the time.

items.b: Cache miss when outcome is unpredictable.
items.html: If the verification outcome is rare or the draft model is weak at predicting outcomes, cache misses spike and the fallback becomes the bottleneck. The entire batch stalls waiting for fallback generation.
If the cache is too large, the draft model spends so much time pre-computing every possible outcome that it becomes the bottleneck, not verification. The parallelism vanishes.

items.b: Weak draft model cannot predict verification outcomes.
items.html: If the draft model and target model disagree heavily on which tokens are likely, the draft's pre-computed outcomes will not match reality, and hits plummet.

Carefully choose the draft model (should be scaled to balance compute with prediction accuracy), tune cache size to the batch size, and use constrained optimization to allocate cache to the most likely outcomes.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny language model inference engine with two models: a small fast draft and a larger slow target. Implement standard speculative decoding and Saguaro. Run both on the same input (e.g. a GPT-2 model on a short prompt), generating 50 tokens. Measure total wall-clock time (latency), number of cache hits, and number of fallback calls. Show that Saguaro's total latency is lower and cache hit rate is high, above 90 percent. Vary the cache budget and show the tradeoff: a small cache costs less compute but misses more often, a large cache hits more often but costs more draft compute. This reveals the hidden quantity: when you spend more compute to make the cache bigger, you hit more often, which means fewer fallbacks and lower total latency.
demo.metric_eq: Total latency = time to generate 50 tokens end-to-end; Cache hit rate = (cache hits) / (total speculations); Speedup = (autoregressive time) / (Saguaro time)
demo.closing: The demo must show that Saguaro's total latency is 2-5x lower than the baseline (generating one token at a time), and that most of the win comes from cache hits eliminating fallback overhead.
